citation: Todd K, Berk WA, Huang R. Effect of body locale and addition of epinephrine on the duration of action of a local anesthetic agent. Ann Emerg Med 1992;21:723-726
text_quality: ok — all four journal pages (723-726) are present with a text layer: abstract, introduction, methods, results, discussion, conclusion, Tables 1-3 with their captions and footnotes, the Figure legend, and all 12 references. Two caveats. (1) The PDF is two-column and the extraction interleaves the columns line by line, so quotes from pages 724-726 are joined with ' … ' at each OCR line break where the other column intervenes; every quote in this card and in the claim updates was checked against texts/S-686-35.txt with the normalisation used by common/tools/quotecheck.py. (2) The Figure is four per-locale line plots of mean score against time with no printed values, so the time courses exist only as plotted points; Table 1 carries the group means, so no numeric result is lost. Scattered OCR noise: letter-spacing inside words ('n o n d o m i n a n t', 'H u m a n'), 'Lidecaine' for 'Lidocaine', 'comt~ared' for 'compared', '_+' for '±', 'i mL' for '1 mL', and superscript reference numerals merged into words ('localeA -a').
design: Two-part open (unblinded) volunteer experiment in the same people, each subject acting as his or her own control across body sites. Experiment 1 (L): plain buffered lidocaine at four body locales in all 20 subjects. Experiment 2 (LE): the same four locales with lidocaine plus epinephrine, on a different day, in ten of the same 20 subjects. No placebo or saline arm, no randomisation of site order reported, no blinding reported, and the two solutions were given on separate days rather than concurrently. Between-locale comparison by repeated-measures ANOVA with the Scheffe test post hoc; plain versus epinephrine comparison by two-tailed paired t-test in the ten subjects who did both phases; mean ratios with 95% confidence intervals for locale-to-face and epinephrine-to-plain.
population: Healthy adult volunteers recruited from emergency department personnel, aged 27 to 48 years (mean 32.0). Exclusions: allergy to lidocaine, pregnancy, and current use of analgesic or sedative agents. Intact, unwounded skin; no neuropathy or other disease state studied.
n: 20 subjects for plain lidocaine at each of the four locales; 10 of those same 20 for lidocaine with epinephrine at each of the four locales. Paired plain-versus-epinephrine comparisons rest on n = 10.
setting: Single centre, Departments of Emergency Medicine, Detroit Receiving Hospital and University Health Center, and Wayne State University, Detroit, Michigan. Approved by the Wayne State University Human Use Committee. Presented at the Society for Academic Emergency Medicine Annual Meeting, Washington DC, May 1991.
intervention: Experiment 1: 1% lidocaine buffered with sodium bicarbonate (buffering method cited to Christoph et al 1988; [preparation detail omitted]), [dose figure omitted] per site. Experiment 2: the same buffered 1% lidocaine containing epinephrine 1:100,000, [dose figure omitted] per site. One deposit per site per experiment; no repeat dosing. The anaesthetic and epinephrine concentrations are recorded here because the paper's own open question asks what this study itself used; the abstract does not state the epinephrine concentration, which is why the full text was needed.
comparator: Two comparisons, both within-subject: (a) three other body locales against the face for the same solution; (b) lidocaine with epinephrine against plain lidocaine at the same locale, in the ten subjects who took part in both phases. There is no placebo, saline or no-injection control.
route: Intradermal — a wheal raised through intact skin with a fine needle on a tuberculin syringe. This is an intradermal weal, not subcutaneous infiltration and not a nerve block. Four sites: forehead close to the scalp; volar forearm just distal to the antecubital fossa; dorsal aspect of the non-dominant hand; and the medial aspect of the leg just below the knee — the site the abstract and Tables call 'calf' and 'Leg' respectively.
duration: Each site followed until anaesthetic effect had gone: assessments every 15 minutes in the plain-lidocaine experiment and every 30 minutes in the epinephrine experiment, continued until no anaesthetic effect was present. Longest mean followed out to about 11.3 hours (leg, with epinephrine, any anaesthesia). Because the first assessment came a fixed interval after injection, onset was not timed. Single session per experiment; the two experiments were on different days.
outcomes: Self-reported response to pinprick at the injection site, marked on a 21-point pain-analysis scale labelled 'dull' at the left margin and 'sharp' at the right, scored 0 (no painful sensation) to 20 (completely absent anaesthetic effect). Two derived endpoints: duration of EFFECTIVE anaesthesia = time until the score exceeded 5; duration of ANY anaesthesia = time until the score exceeded 19, i.e. essentially complete return of sensation. Secondary: mean ratios of duration between locales and between solutions, with 95% confidence intervals.

studies_it_cites_that_matter.citation: Christoph RA, Buchanan L, Begalla K, Schwartz S. Pain reduction in local anesthetic administration through pH buffering. Ann Emerg Med 1988;17:117-120
studies_it_cites_that_matter.why: The most important reference in this paper for the job. Todd cites it only for the buffering method, but Europe PMC shows one of its three arms was lidocaine with epinephrine at the same anaesthetic and epinephrine strengths as Todd's second experiment, given by intradermal injection in a randomised, prospective, double-blind study of 25 adult volunteers, with onset, extent and duration of skin anaesthesia recorded. It is therefore a second study refuting C081, and the only one of the three that measures onset. The record already cites it at D025 (mepivacaine arm) and D012 (pH comparison) without noticing this arm. Todd's reference list prints the third author as 'Begalia K'; Europe PMC has 'Begalla K'.

studies_it_cites_that_matter.citation: Swerdlow M, Jones R. The duration of action of bupivacaine, prilocaine and lignocaine. Br J Anaesth 1970;42:335-339
studies_it_cites_that_matter.why: The randomised intradermal skin-weal duration study of three anaesthetics with and without adrenaline that C039 lists among the seven papers never opened. Verified in Europe PMC: publication types Randomized Controlled Trial, Clinical Trial and Comparative Study, MeSH Injections, Intradermal; Skin Tests; Epinephrine administration & dosage; no abstract indexed; 43 citing papers. Already the primary paper of another worker in this job (S-686-31, for D009), so not re-judged here. Its presence in Todd's reference list places Todd inside the same intradermal-weal tradition that C031 describes.

studies_it_cites_that_matter.citation: Wightman MA, Vaughan RW. Comparison of compounds used for intradermal anesthesia. Anesthesiology 1976;45:687-689
studies_it_cites_that_matter.why: The human intradermal preservative comparison behind C038 and C039; already the primary paper of another worker (S-686-39). Cited by Todd as previous single-locale duration work, which again ties Todd to the intradermal-weal literature the record treats as uncited by modern reviews.

studies_it_cites_that_matter.citation: Gramling ZW, Ellis RG Jr, Volpitto PP. Clinical experiences with mepivacaine (carbocaine). J Med Assoc Ga 1964;53:16-18
studies_it_cites_that_matter.why: A candidate origin for an old mepivacaine duration figure relevant to D025, looked up and set aside: Europe PMC indexes no abstract and no DOI, and its MeSH terms point to conduction anaesthesia rather than skin, so it cannot be shown to be a skin-duration measurement.

studies_it_cites_that_matter.citation: Barone JA, Weisman R, Mangione RA, Goldfrank LR. Serum lidocaine concentrations following subcutaneous administration. Clin Pharm 1984;3:281-284
studies_it_cites_that_matter.why: The study Todd uses at page 725 to argue that wounding itself may change duration: 30 patients having lacerations repaired, sampled at 15 to 60 minutes, with the authors concluding absorption appears altered in traumatised tissue. It is the published basis for Todd's own caution that its intact-skin volunteer figures may not transfer to wounded tissue, which matters wherever this record reads Todd's durations across to a clinical setting. Paired by Todd with Nattel 1979 (PMID 460344) for the intact-skin contrast. Any claim these two would otherwise decide has a dose ceiling or plasma threshold as its subject, so the brief's writing rules require them to be counted rather than written out.

studies_it_cites_that_matter.citation: Magee C, Rodeheaver GT, Edgerton MT, Golden GT, Haury B, Edlich RF. Studies of the mechanisms by which epinephrine damages tissue defenses. J Surg Res 1977;23:126-131
studies_it_cites_that_matter.why: One of the two papers Todd cites for epinephrine potentiating infection. A rabbit study of host defence (phagocytosis, immunity, blood bactericidal activity) with phentolamine as a blocking comparator; single exposure, no nerve or tissue histology, no concentration in the indexing. It does not refute C075 or C093 and supports the existing reading that the nearest animal work is single-exposure and about wound defence rather than innervation.

studies_it_cites_that_matter.citation: Stevenson TR, Rodeheaver GT, Golden GT, et al. Damage to tissue defenses by vasoconstrictors. JACEP 1975;4:532-535
studies_it_cites_that_matter.why: The second epinephrine-and-infection citation. Not resolvable: two Europe PMC title searches returned hitCount 0, so no PMID was confirmed and the abstract could not be read. PMID left blank rather than guessed.

studies_it_cites_that_matter.citation: McCafferty DF, Woolfson AD, Boston V. In vivo assessment of percutaneous local anaesthetic preparations. Br J Anaesth 1989;62:17-21
studies_it_cites_that_matter.why: Cited by Todd as previous duration work, but it is a topical percutaneous comparison of an amethocaine preparation against EMLA, so it does not bear on any intradermal-injection claim. Recorded to show the reference was checked and set aside on route.

studies_it_cites_that_matter.citation: Scott J, Huskisson EC: Graphic representation of pain. Pain 1976;2:175-181
studies_it_cites_that_matter.why: The methodological source for Todd's 21-point pain-analysis scale, which is how its duration endpoints were defined. Relevant only to how the endpoint should be read: Todd's durations are self-reported pinprick scores on a visual-analogue-style line, not an examiner-blinded sensory test. PMID not looked up; it decides no claim.

studies_it_cites_that_matter.citation: Berk WA, Osbourne DB, Taylor DD: Evaluation of the "golden period" for wound repair: 204 cases for a third world emergency department. Ann Emerg Med 1988;17:496-500
studies_it_cites_that_matter.why: A self-citation by the second author, on wound infection timing. Noted only for the author-overlap screen; it bears on no claim in claims_all.json. Gravett 1987 (povidone-iodine in sutured lacerations, Ann Emerg Med 1987;16:167-171) is cited alongside it for the same point and is likewise outside the claim set.
